rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, 3-year field experiment at Citra FL on Candler/Tavares sand with root sampling in 2006. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 5, root length density under all drip treatments concentrated around the irrigation/fertigation emitter, with a 41% reduction in RLD from the drip line (P1) to 0.125 m (P2) and 70% from P1 to 0.25 m (P3); Fig. 5 shows SMS-based drip roots confined to upper 20-30 cm. Q9: Section 3.3, RLD at P1 (0-15 cm, 66 DAT) reported as 10.5 +/- 3.9 for SDI versus 2.6 +/- 1.7 and 2.5 +/- 0.9 cm cm-3 for SUR and TIME (standard deviations).
rows.notes: Study has no non-drip comparison; all treatments are drip. It documents root concentration near emitters on a sandy soil, which supports the claim only descriptively. Limited lateral water movement is asserted as a general property of coarse sands (Section 3.1), not measured laterally: TDR and nitrate samples were at 0.05-0.10 m from the drip line only, so Q4 no. Root data from one site, one crop, one season (2006), one N-rate; no stated limitations of the root result. Nutrient interception at bed sides not measured.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own 3-year field experiment. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 2, soil-moisture-sensor-controlled drip (SUR, SDI, up to five short daily events) increased marketable yield 69-80% (2005), 20-26% (2006), 11-21% (2007) versus fixed-time daily irrigation; above-ground biomass also higher. Q4: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, TDR soil water showed relatively constant soil moisture under SMS treatments versus large spikes and rapid percolation under TIME; Section 3.3, residual soil nitrate in 0-30 cm was 32 and 12 mg kg-1 for SDI and SUR versus 2 for TIME, linking frequent small applications to water/N retention and yield. Q8: Section 3.2 and Conclusions, authors restrict the 11-26% yield gain to 2006-2007 when weather was not yield-limiting, noting 2005 results were affected by bacterial spot disease, high temperature and rain.
rows.notes: Yield measured by one method (plot harvest); no triangulation. Single site, soil and crop over 3 years. Crop water stress itself not measured (no plant water status). Table 1 gives CV% for yield and letter groupings only; no SD/CI for treatment means, so Q9 no. No condition stated as a requirement for the yield effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment with TDR soil water monitoring and biweekly soil nitrate sampling at three depths. Q2: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, SMS-based short irrigations produced small soil moisture increases and almost no spikes at 25-55 cm, while TIME produced pronounced spikes with percolation to deeper layers; Section 3.3, soil nitrate at 74 DAT in 0-30 cm was 32 (SDI) and 12 (SUR) versus 2 mg kg-1 (TIME), authors state TIME leaching was often very intense leaving soil N invariably low. Q3: two independent lines of own data, TDR soil water dynamics at two depths (Fig. 4) and KCl-extracted soil nitrate profiles (Section 3.3), both indicating reduced leaching under SMS control. Q4: Fig. 4 and Section 3.1, drainage/percolation spikes in soil water content measured under TIME versus their absence under SMS treatments. Q8: Section 3.1, authors state that because of the TDR probe position (0-25 cm) relative to the buried drip line, soil moisture variations for SDI were not as distinct, limiting interpretation for that treatment.
rows.notes: Leaching was not measured directly (no lysimeter or leachate collection); it is inferred from soil water spikes and residual soil nitrate, so Q2/Q3 are a cautious yes. Soil nitrate values given as single means without SD, so Q9 no. One site, soil and crop. No condition stated as a requirement for the leaching reduction.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own 3-year field experiment. Q2: Abstract, Section 3.1, Fig. 2 and Conclusions, SMS-controlled surface drip (SUR) applied 15-51% less irrigation water than fixed-time irrigation and SMS-controlled SDI 7-29% less, with yields higher than TIME. Q4: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, controller bypassed events when soil water was at or above the 0.10 m3 m-3 threshold; TDR data show TIME exceeded soil water holding capacity with percolation while SMS treatments kept soil moisture near constant. Q8: Section 3.1 and Conclusions, authors state SDI savings were low because the soil moisture probe was positioned the same as for SUR and averaged a relatively dry top 15 cm above the buried drip line, so fewer events were bypassed and more water was applied.
rows.notes: Review's figures (40-65% savings, 11-45% yield) do not match the study (SUR 40-51% in 2006-2007, 15% in 2005; SDI 7-29%; yield 11-80%). Irrigation volume measured by flowmeters only (one method). Probe placement relative to the drip line is given as an explanation ('may be attributed'), not explicitly stated as a requirement, so Q7 no with doubt. Savings reported as ranges across years and CV% for iWUE only; no SD/CI, so Q9 no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 2, SMS-controlled drip treatments (SUR, SDI) increased marketable tomato yield 69-80%, 20-26% and 11-21% over fixed-time irrigation in 2005, 2006 and 2007, with higher above-ground biomass. Q4: Fig. 4 and Section 3.3, soil water dynamics (no percolation spikes under SMS) and residual soil nitrate (32 and 12 versus 2 mg kg-1 in 0-30 cm) measured as the pathway from scheduling to yield. Q8: Conclusions and Section 3.2, authors restrict the 11-26% yield increase to 2006-2007 when weather was not yield-limiting and describe disease and heat effects in 2005.
rows.notes: Review's 11-45% yield range does not match the study's 11-80%. Yield from plot harvest only; single site, soil and crop. Table 1 reports CV% and Table 2 letter groupings; no SD/CI for yield means, so Q9 no. No requirement for the effect stated from own findings.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, 3-year small-plot field trial on fresh-market tomato. Q2: Abstract, Fig. 2 and Conclusions, ECH2O capacitance probe-controlled drip irrigation (SUR) used 15-51% and SDI 7-29% less irrigation water than daily fixed-time irrigation. Q4: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, soil water content monitored by TDR showed bypassed events kept moisture near threshold under SMS while TIME produced spikes above holding capacity and percolation. Q8: Section 3.1 and Conclusions, authors state the SDI water savings were reduced by the probe position relative to the buried drip line, which led to fewer bypassed events.
rows.notes: Study matches the claim well (capacitance sensors, drip tomato, small plots, Florida sand). One measurement method (flowmeters). Single site/crop/soil. No SD/CI on water savings (ranges across years only). Probe placement is explanatory, not stated as a requirement, so Q7 no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own small-plot field trial. Q2: Table 2 and Section 3.2, capacitance-sensor-controlled drip treatments increased marketable tomato yield 11-80% over fixed-time irrigation across 2005-2007 and raised above-ground biomass. Q4: Fig. 4 and Section 3.3, soil water dynamics and residual soil nitrate measured, with higher nitrate retention in 0-30 cm under SMS treatments offered as the pathway to higher yield. Q8: Conclusions and Section 3.2, yield gain of 11-26% stated as applying to 2006-2007 when weather was not yield-limiting, with 2005 affected by disease and heat.
rows.notes: Yield by plot harvest only; one site, soil and crop over three seasons. Only CV% and letter groupings reported for yield, no SD/CI (Q9 no). No requirement for the yield effect stated from own results.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a 3-year factorial field experiment (3 irrigation scheduling treatments x 3 N rates) on tomato on sandy soil in Florida; SMS-controlled surface and subsurface drip versus fixed-time daily drip. Leaching is inferred from TDR soil water dynamics and residual soil nitrate rather than measured directly. Several review-cited numbers (40-65% savings, 11-45% yield) differ from the study's own figures.
